questions.q: What is the key factor that decides whether a payment should be voided or stopped?
options: The amount of the payment
Whether the payment has already been issued/sent, and whether it has cleared the bank
Whether the supplier is domestic or international
Whether the invoice was two-way or three-way matched
questions.explain: Void applies before a payment leaves the organization's control; stop payment applies after it's issued but before it clears.

questions.q: What additional step does a stop payment require that a void does not?
options: A new purchase order
A new supplier record
Action with the bank itself to place a hold on the check or transaction
A new matching tolerance set
questions.explain: Unlike a void, which is purely internal to Oracle, a stop payment requires contacting the bank to place a hold on that specific item.

questions.q: In the Harbor Point Logistics example, the lost check is confirmed not to have cleared. What is done first?
options: A stop payment is placed with the bank on that check
The invoice is immediately cancelled with no payment
The supplier is removed from the system
A new purchase order is created
questions.explain: Since the check had already been sent but hadn't cleared, a stop payment (not a void) is the correct action.

questions.q: What happens to the underlying invoice when a payment is voided or stopped?
options: It is permanently cancelled and cannot be paid
Nothing changes -- the invoice remains marked as paid
It is automatically converted into a credit memo
It reverts to an unpaid status, ready to be picked up again
questions.explain: Both voiding and stopping return the related invoice to unpaid status so it can be reissued or picked up in a future payment run.

options: Deleting the original invoice permanently
Creating a brand-new payment for the same invoices, often with a different payment method
Sending the exact same check a second time without any changes
Reversing the supplier's bank account details
questions.explain: Reissuing creates a replacement payment for the same underlying invoices, sometimes switching the payment method to avoid repeating the original problem.
